decisions.account:
The archive contains only the baseline harness (score 0.0), which is a plain ReAct loop: every tool result lands verbatim in the transcript until the context fills, and nothing checks the final answer against what the agent actually found. This design adds an **external evidence ledger** as a new component (`middleware/ledger.py`, plus `tools/note_evidence.py`, `tools/read_notes.py`, their schemas, `agent.yaml`, and rewritten `prompts/system.md` + `skills/main.md`).

What it does differently: (1) `note_evidence` is intercepted by the middleware's `before_tool` hook, so writing a finding costs **no LLM round trip** — the model gets a compact map of its evidence back immediately, with dedupe/merge on restatement (re-confirming evidence moves the note to "fresh") and an explicit `keep_separate` flag for contradicting versions. Notes live in `ctx.state`, never in the prompt, and are read back only on demand. (2) `after_tool` replaces oversized results (search listings, page extracts, file/shell dumps) with a head+tail **preview** that is saved in full to `runs/.../artifacts/`, so the model is told "the raw text will not stay — note the values you need now". This keeps the working set small and forces distilled state instead of hoarded text, which should shift turns from re-reading to reasoning. (3) `before_final` runs one side-LLM consistency check of the draft against the stored notes only, and on a specific contradiction/format gap returns `continue` with targeted feedback (capped by the kernel's existing budget) rather than a generic "try again". Prompts teach the discipline: state the answer's expected form first, note every exact value with its source the moment it is visible, note dead ends so they aren't retried, and consult `read_notes` before answering.

Why it should score higher: the two dominant failure modes of a truncation-free ReAct loop on held-out QA/research/editing tasks are losing early findings to context pressure and shipping an answer that contradicts the agent's own evidence. The ledger addresses both without hard-coding any task, and every hook is a no-op when the model never takes a note — so it cannot regress a run that already worked. Verified locally with stubbed LLMs: merge/dedupe, conflict, gap classification, truncation+artifact save, on-demand retrieval, revised-answer loop, empty-ledger accept, and max-turns forced answer.

Uncertainty: samples=1 per task and a single task in the invariant; score 1.0 on train:0 is a binary pass, so the delta 0.0 has essentially no resolving power — it is consistent with identical, slightly better, or slightly worse behavior on unseen inputs. Statements that "the accepted answer is unchanged" are an argument about mechanism, not a measurement. Fidelity=screen and one unverified prompt edit further cap confidence. Do not treat this as evidence of statistical equivalence between parent and candidate.

Next hypothesis: mutations at score ceiling should be judged by coverage, cost, and no-op rate rather than by delta. Concretely: (1) restrict normalization to a narrow, test-anchored trigger (e.g., only when the answer is a single line with no internal punctuation and the task requested a bare entity) and add counterexample fixtures to the invariant — exact-spelling names, quoted titles, one-line JSON, and an "Answer: X" label case — so a wrap-stripping bug would surface as regression mass; (2) more usefully, re-target effort at a dimension this task does not test, e.g., selecting the answer when near-miss distractors conflict or when only prose (no structured record) supports it, and measure on tasks containing such conflict; (3) split skill/prompt/runtime changes into separate candidates so the neutral composite can be attributed rather than averaged.
</LEARNINGS>
